```{ojs}
//| output: false
// VM is the shared utility library, loaded globally via _includes/head-scripts.html (js/**). This page uses VM.sampling.seededRandom, VM.expressions.makeNumber, VM.ui.renderTable.
VM = window.VM
```

```{ojs}
//| output: false
// URL preset helpers for examples.
// Supported query parameters:
//   n       number of states
//   seed    random seed for the transition matrix draw
//   start   starting state (1-indexed)
//   max     maximum steps
urlParams = new URLSearchParams(window.location.search)

maxN = 6

initialN = {
  const raw = Number(urlParams.get("n"))
  return Number.isInteger(raw) && raw >= 2 && raw <= maxN ? raw : 4
}

initialSeed = {
  const raw = Number(urlParams.get("seed"))
  return Number.isInteger(raw) && raw >= 0 ? raw : 11
}

initialStart = {
  const raw = Number(urlParams.get("start"))
  return Number.isInteger(raw) && raw >= 1 ? raw : 1
}

initialMax = urlParams.get("max") ?? "30"
```

<div class="ojs-panel ojs-row">

```{ojs}
viewof n = {
  const input = Inputs.range([2, maxN], {step: 1, value: initialN, label: "Number of states"})
  input.classList.add("ojs-fill")
  return input
}
```

```{ojs}
viewof startStateNumber = {
  const input = Inputs.range([1, n], {step: 1, value: Math.min(initialStart, n), label: "Starting state"})
  input.classList.add("ojs-fill")
  return input
}
```

<div class="ojs-panel ojs-row">

```{ojs}
viewof seedValue = {
  const input = Inputs.number({value: initialSeed, min: 0, step: 1, label: "Random seed"})
  input.classList.add("ojs-auto")
  return input
}
```

```{ojs}
// regenerateTrigger: clicking "Regenerate transition matrix" bumps this,
// the only thing transitionMatrix depends on below — that's what makes a
// fresh draw happen on click instead of only once at page load.
viewof regenerateTrigger = {
  const button = Inputs.button("Regenerate transition matrix", {value: 0, reduce: v => v + 1})
  button.classList.add("ojs-auto")
  return button
}
```

</div>

<div class="ojs-panel ojs-row">

```{ojs}
viewof stepControl = {
  const maxStep = Math.max(0, result.rows.length - 1)
  const stepSlider = Inputs.range([0, maxStep], {step: 1, value: 0, label: "Step"})
  stepSlider.classList.add("ojs-fill")
  return stepSlider
}
```

```{ojs}
viewof maxStepsInput = {
  const input = Inputs.text({value: initialMax, label: "Max steps", placeholder: "Example: 30, 5*6"})
  input.classList.add("ojs-auto")
  return input
}
```

</div>

```{ojs}
//| output: false
// maxSteps parses the Max field's expression, falling back to 30 for
// invalid input so the step slider and result loop always get a usable bound.
maxSteps = {
  const math = window.math
  const parsed = VM.expressions.makeNumber(math, maxStepsInput)
  if (parsed === null || !Number.isFinite(parsed)) return 30
  return Math.max(1, Math.round(parsed))
}
```

```{ojs}
//| output: false
startState = startStateNumber - 1
```

```{ojs}
//| output: false
// Keeps n, seed, starting state, and max steps shareable as the reactive
// controls change.
urlSyncControls = {
  const params = new URLSearchParams(window.location.search)
  params.set("n", String(n))
  params.set("seed", String(seedValue))
  params.set("start", String(startStateNumber))
  params.set("max", maxStepsInput)
  history.replaceState(null, "", `${window.location.pathname}?${params}`)
  return true
}
```

```{ojs}
//| output: false
// transitionMatrix: an n×n row-stochastic matrix (each row sums to 1),
// drawn fresh whenever the seed, regenerate count, or n changes. Every
// entry gets a +0.05 floor before normalizing so no transition probability
// is ever exactly (or nearly) zero — this keeps the chain irreducible and
// aperiodic (every state reachable from every other, no forced cycles),
// which is exactly what guarantees a unique stationary distribution exists
// and every starting state converges to it.
transitionMatrix = {
  regenerateTrigger
  const rand = VM.sampling.seededRandom((Math.floor(seedValue) + regenerateTrigger * 1000003 + n * 131) >>> 0)
  const rows = []
  for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    const raw = []
    let sum = 0
    for (let j = 0; j < n; j++) {
      const v = rand() + 0.05
      raw.push(v)
      sum += v
    }
    const row = []
    for (let j = 0; j < n; j++) row.push(raw[j] / sum)
    rows.push(row)
  }
  return rows
}
```

```{ojs}
//| output: false
// statePositions: states placed evenly around a fixed circle — no
// force-directed layout needed for a handful of nodes, just simple
// trigonometry. Position i is at angle -90° + i * 360°/n, so state 1
// starts at the top and the rest go clockwise.
statePositions = {
  const radius = 5
  const positions = []
  for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    const angle = -Math.PI / 2 + (2 * Math.PI * i) / n
    positions.push({x: radius * Math.cos(angle), y: radius * Math.sin(angle)})
  }
  return positions
}
```

```{ojs}
//| output: false
// stepDistribution: one step of π ↦ πP — a row-vector/matrix product.
function stepDistribution(dist, matrix) {
  const size = matrix.length
  const next = new Array(size).fill(0)
  for (let i = 0; i < size; i++) {
    const pi = dist[i]
    if (pi === 0) continue
    for (let j = 0; j < size; j++) next[j] += pi * matrix[i][j]
  }
  return next
}
```

```{ojs}
//| output: false
// stationaryDistribution: the reference π* that result's rows are measured
// against, found by power iteration — repeatedly applying π ↦ πP from a
// neutral (uniform) start until it settles. This is the same power-
// iteration idea used to find a dominant eigenvector elsewhere; here it's
// converging to the left eigenvector of the transition matrix for
// eigenvalue 1. Computed once per transitionMatrix, independent of
// whatever starting state/step the controls above are set to.
stationaryDistribution = {
  let dist = new Array(n).fill(1 / n)
  for (let t = 0; t < 500; t++) dist = stepDistribution(dist, transitionMatrix)
  return dist
}
```

```{ojs}
//| output: false
// result: runs the chain from a one-hot distribution at the starting
// state. rows[t].dist is the distribution AT step t (before the step-t→t+1
// update is applied) — same "row records the state a step saw" convention
// as Newton's method's x_n. rows[t].distance is the total variation
// distance ‖dist − stationaryDistribution‖₁ at that step, used by the
// convergence plot below.
result = {
  if (n < 1) return {rows: []}
  const start = Math.min(Math.max(startState, 0), n - 1)
  let dist = new Array(n).fill(0)
  dist[start] = 1

  const rows = []
  for (let t = 0; t <= maxSteps; t++) {
    let distance = 0
    for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) distance += Math.abs(dist[i] - stationaryDistribution[i])
    rows.push({t, dist: dist.slice(), distance})
    dist = stepDistribution(dist, transitionMatrix)
  }
  return {rows}
}
```

```{ojs}
//| output: false
setup = {
  if (result.rows.length === 0) return {row: null}
  const step = Math.min(Math.max(Math.round(Number(stepControl)), 0), result.rows.length - 1)
  return {row: result.rows[step]}
}
```

```{ojs}
// stepStatus: a short line above the plot reporting the current step's
// distance from the stationary distribution.
stepStatus = {
  if (!setup.row) return html`<div class="ojs-panel">No chain to show.</div>`
  const row = setup.row
  return html`<div class="ojs-panel"><strong>Step ${row.t}</strong> of ${result.rows.length - 1} — total variation distance to the stationary distribution: ${row.distance.toFixed(4)}.</div>`
}
```

```{ojs}
//| output: false
// mainPlot draws the state graph: nodes placed on a fixed circle, sized
// and colored by how much probability mass is currently there, with
// directed edges (arrows) for every transition probability above a small
// visibility threshold — width and opacity both scale with the
// probability, so a dense, high-traffic edge reads as bold and a rare one
// fades into the background instead of disappearing outright.
//
// _plotDiv is kept in a closure so Plotly reuses the same DOM node across
// reactive updates — this preserves zoom and pan when the step changes.
// Note this factory closure only reads `Plotly`/`_plotDiv` — `row`,
// `matrix`, and `positions` all arrive as call-time parameters instead of
// being referenced directly from outer reactive cells, which is what lets
// Plotly.react (not a fresh div) handle every update.
mainPlot = {
  const Plotly = window.Plotly
  let _plotDiv = null
  const edgeThreshold = 0.03

  return ({row, matrix, positions}) => {
    const data = []
    const annotations = []

    if (row) {
      const size = positions.length

      for (let i = 0; i < size; i++) {
        for (let j = 0; j < size; j++) {
          if (i === j) continue
          const p = matrix[i][j]
          if (p < edgeThreshold) continue
          annotations.push({
            x: positions[j].x, y: positions[j].y,
            ax: positions[i].x, ay: positions[i].y,
            xref: "x", yref: "y", axref: "x", ayref: "y",
            showarrow: true, arrowhead: 2, arrowsize: 1,
            arrowwidth: Math.max(1, p * 5),
            opacity: Math.min(1, 0.25 + p * 0.75),
            arrowcolor: "#64748b",
            standoff: 16, startstandoff: 16
          })
        }
      }

      const xs = [], ys = [], sizes = [], colors = [], hoverTexts = [], labels = []
      for (let i = 0; i < size; i++) {
        xs.push(positions[i].x)
        ys.push(positions[i].y)
        const mass = row.dist[i]
        sizes.push(24 + mass * 60)
        colors.push(mass)
        labels.push(String(i + 1))
        hoverTexts.push(`State ${i + 1}<br>P(here) = ${mass.toFixed(3)}<br>P(stay) = ${matrix[i][i].toFixed(3)}`)
      }

      data.push({
        x: xs, y: ys, type: "scatter", mode: "markers+text",
        text: labels, textposition: "middle center", textfont: {color: "#111827", size: 13},
        hovertext: hoverTexts, hoverinfo: "text",
        marker: {
          size: sizes, color: colors, colorscale: [[0, "#dbeafe"], [1, "#1d4ed8"]],
          cmin: 0, cmax: 1, line: {color: "#111827", width: 1.5}
        },
        showlegend: false
      })
    }

    const layout = {
      margin: {l: 10, r: 10, t: 10, b: 10},
      xaxis: {visible: false, range: [-7, 7]},
      // scaleanchor/scaleratio lock the y-axis to the same scale as x, so
      // the circular layout renders as an actual circle.
      yaxis: {visible: false, range: [-7, 7], scaleanchor: "x", scaleratio: 1},
      annotations,
      hovermode: "closest",
      uirevision: "static",
      autosize: true
    }
    const config = {responsive: true, displaylogo: false}

    if (!_plotDiv) {
      _plotDiv = document.createElement("div")
      _plotDiv.className = "plotly-box-large"
      Plotly.newPlot(_plotDiv, data, layout, config)
      // newPlot fires before the div is in the DOM, so Plotly measures 0 width.
      // A ResizeObserver catches the real size once it's inserted and laid out,
      // and keeps correcting it on any later layout/viewport change.
      new ResizeObserver(() => Plotly.Plots.resize(_plotDiv)).observe(_plotDiv)
    } else {
      Plotly.react(_plotDiv, data, layout, config)
    }
    return _plotDiv
  }
}
```

```{ojs}
// iteratesPlot draws every state's probability vs step for the entire
// run — it doesn't depend on the current step, so it's just plotted once
// per run. Regardless of which state the chain started in, every line
// should approach the same long-run value: the stationary distribution.
iteratesPlot = {
  const rows = []
  for (const row of result.rows) {
    for (let i = 0; i < row.dist.length; i++) {
      rows.push({t: row.t, state: `State ${i + 1}`, p: row.dist[i]})
    }
  }
  return Plot.plot({
    width: 340, height: 300, marginLeft: 46,
    x: {label: "step"},
    y: {label: "P(state) at step t", domain: [0, 1]},
    color: {legend: true},
    marks: [
      Plot.lineY(rows, {x: "t", y: "p", stroke: "state"})
    ]
  })
}
```

```{ojs}
// convergencePlot draws log₁₀ of the total variation distance to the
// stationary distribution vs step — the standard "how far from done" plot
// (same idea as Newton's/bisection's log-error convergence plots).
// Markov chain convergence is geometric, so this is roughly a straight
// line once the chain settles into its dominant convergence rate.
convergencePlot = {
  const rows = []
  for (const row of result.rows) {
    if (row.distance > 0) rows.push({t: row.t, y: Math.log10(row.distance)})
  }
  return Plot.plot({
    width: 340, height: 300, marginLeft: 46,
    x: {label: "step"},
    y: {label: "log₁₀ (distance to stationary)"},
    marks: [
      Plot.lineY(rows, {x: "t", y: "y", stroke: "#dc2626"}),
      Plot.dot(rows, {x: "t", y: "y", fill: "#dc2626", r: 3})
    ]
  })
}
```

:::

```{ojs}
// transitionMatrixTable shows the raw numbers behind the graph above —
// row i, column j is P(state i → state j).
transitionMatrixTable = {
  const headers = ["From \\ To"]
  for (let j = 0; j < n; j++) headers.push(`State ${j + 1}`)

  const rows = []
  for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    const row = [`State ${i + 1}`]
    for (let j = 0; j < n; j++) row.push(transitionMatrix[i][j].toFixed(3))
    rows.push(row)
  }

  return VM.ui.renderTable({
    html,
    headers,
    csvHeaders: headers,
    filename: "markov-chain-transition-matrix.csv",
    rows
  })
}
```

```{ojs}
// Iteration table — shows the entire run, not just the current step.
iterationTable = {
  if (result.rows.length === 0) {
    // Always return a Node so Quarto's OJS runtime never latches this
    // declaration cell as hidden.
    return document.createElement("div")
  }

  const headers = ["Step"]
  for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) headers.push(`P(State ${i + 1})`)
  headers.push("Distance to stationary")

  const rows = []
  for (const row of result.rows) {
    const r = [row.t]
    for (let i = 0; i < row.dist.length; i++) r.push(row.dist[i].toFixed(4))
    r.push(row.distance.toExponential(3))
    rows.push(r)
  }

  return VM.ui.renderTable({
    html,
    headers,
    csvHeaders: headers,
    filename: "markov-chain-steps.csv",
    rows
  })
}
```

</div>

A Markov chain moves between $n$ states; the probability of moving from state $i$ to state $j$ is a fixed number $P_{ij}$, independent of how the chain got to $i$. Writing the current distribution over states as a row vector $\pi_t$, one step forward is a vector-matrix product:

$$
\pi_{t+1} = \pi_t P.
$$

A **stationary distribution** $\pi^*$ is a fixed point of this update: $\pi^* = \pi^* P$, with $\sum_i \pi^*_i = 1$. As long as every state can reach every other state and the chain isn't forced into a rigid cycle (true here, since every transition probability is generated strictly positive), $\pi^*$ is unique — and $\pi_t \to \pi^*$ as $t \to \infty$, **no matter which state the chain started in**.

## Why this matters

Try different starting states at the same seed: every one of them settles into the exact same distribution shown by the node colors, even though they start from completely different (one-hot) distributions. That's the content of the convergence theorem above — the chain "forgets" where it started. The rate it forgets at is visible in the convergence plot: a steeper downward line means the chain mixes faster (reaches its long-run behavior sooner), a shallower one means it mixes slowly, lingering near its starting state for longer before letting go.

The node sizes and colors are just $\pi_t$ redrawn as a picture: a state that's easy to reach (heavy inbound arrows) and hard to leave (a high self-loop probability, shown in its hover text) ends up with more long-run probability mass than one that's a temporary waypoint on the way somewhere else. With more states and a denser graph, watch how probability spends longer sloshing around before settling — that's the same mixing-time idea, just harder to eyeball directly from the graph alone, which is exactly why the convergence plot exists.
